title: Compact projective complex geometry and its Fubini--Study metric
statement:
Let $n\geq0$, work over $\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field], and define $P=\mathbf P^n(\mathbf C)$ as the quotient of $\mathbf C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}$ by multiplication by nonzero scalars, with the quotient topology and the standard holomorphic charts $U_j=\{[z]:z_j\ne0\}$, $[z]\mapsto(z_k/z_j)_{k\ne j}$. Then $P$ is a compact Hausdorff second-countable complex manifold without boundary of complex dimension $n$. The quotient map $\pi:\mathbf C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}\to P$ is holomorphic; each $U_j$ has a holomorphic section $s_j:U_j\to\mathbf C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}$, obtained by setting coordinate $j$ to $1$, with $\pi\circ s_j=\mathrm{id}_{U_j}$. In chart coordinates $w=(w_1,\ldots,w_n)$ the real $(1,1)$-forms
$$\omega_j=\frac{i}{2\pi}\partial\bar\partial\log(1+\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^n|w_k|^2)$$
glue to a smooth real closed $(1,1)$-form $\omega$ on $P$ that is positive definite: $\omega(v,Jv)>0$ for every nonzero real tangent vector $v$, where $J$ is multiplication by $i$. Equivalently $g(v,w)=\omega(v,Jw)$ is a positive definite Hermitian metric with associated form $\omega$, so $P$ is Kähler. For $n=0$ this is the zero form and the unique metric on the zero-dimensional tangent bundle; positivity has no nonzero vector to test.

source.place: WANTED locally: Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry, V §15.A opening, printed p.277 (quotient, compactness, charts and sections), VI §4 Example (4.4), printed p.297 (Fubini--Study). proof.text:
Put $Z=\mathbf C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}$. The quotient map is open: for open $O\subset Z$, its saturation is $\pi^{-1}\pi(O)= igcup_{\lambda
e0}\lambda O$, open since multiplication by fixed $\lambda
e0$ is a homeomorphism. Thus $U_j$ is open and $\pi:\{z_j
e0\}	o U_j$ is a quotient map. The ratios $z_k/z_j$ are constant on its fibres and are continuous by [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-function-operations]; hence they descend to a continuous map $	au_j:U_j	o\mathbf C^n$. The continuous map $w\mapsto\pi(s_j(w))$, with $s_j(w)_j=1$ and $s_j(w)_k=w_k$, is its inverse, as dividing a representative by $z_j$ gives exactly this representative. These charts cover $P$. Pull back the balls with positive rational radii and centres in $(\mathbf Q+i\mathbf Q)^n$ along each $	au_j$. They form a countable basis: for any open $O$ and $x\in O$, choose $j$ with $x\in U_j$ and a rational ball containing $	au_j(x)$ inside $	au_j(O\cap U_j)$. Thus $P$ is second-countable.

proof.text: For Hausdorffness define $A([z])_{rs}=z_r\bar z_s/\sum_k|z_k|^2$. Its entries descend continuously from $Z$ by the definition of quotient topology; their denominator is strictly positive. Acting on a column $a$, this matrix gives $z(\sum_s\bar z_s a_s)/\|z\|^2$, so its range is precisely $\mathbf C z$ (it fixes $z$). Consequently equal matrices give equal lines. For two distinct points an entry has distinct real or imaginary parts. Choose disjoint real open intervals around these two values; their inverse images under that continuous real-valued entry are disjoint open neighbourhoods. This proves Hausdorffness without assuming that an arbitrary quotient is Hausdorff.

source.place: V §15.A, the Hausdorff assertion in the projective-manifold construction; explicit separating functions supplied by N8; read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/agbook.pdf (local copy WANTED).

proof.text: Regard $\mathbf C^{n+1}$ as the finite-dimensional real normed vector space with the $2n+2$ coordinate vectors $e_j,ie_j$. The unit sphere $S$ is compact in its subspace topology by [lem-cbc-euclidean-sphere-compact]. Its map to $P$ induced by $\pi$ is continuous and onto, since any nonzero $z$ is equivalent to $z/\|z\|\in S$. Given an open cover of $P$, its inverse images form an open cover of $S$. A finite subcover of $S$ gives a finite subcover of $P$ by surjectivity, which is exactly compactness.

proof.text:
On $U_j\cap U_l$, write $a=s_j(w)$, so $a_j=1$. The coordinate change is $	au_l	au_j^{-1}(w)=(a_k/a_l)_{k
e l}$ on $a_l
e0$, with the same formula exchanging $j,l$ for its inverse. These functions are holomorphic by [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-function-operations], so the charts define a complex manifold of dimension $n$ without boundary (their targets are all of $\mathbf C^n$). The expression for $\pi$ in chart $j$ is $(z_k/z_j)_{k
e j}$ on $z_j
e0$, hence holomorphic by the same node. In these coordinates the section $s_j$ is affine-linear, hence holomorphic; its $j$th coordinate is $1$, so it lies in $Z$ and $\pi s_j=\mathrm{id}$.

proof.text: Set $t_j=\|s_j(w)\|^2=1+\sum_{k\ne j}|w_k|^2$ and $\phi_j=\log t_j$, a smooth real function since $t_j\geq1$. Define $\omega_j=D\phi_j$ using [lem-sfb-local-ddbar-potential-calculus]. For the change $F=\tau_l\tau_j^{-1}$ above, $s_l(F(w))=s_j(w)/a_l$, whence $\phi_l\circ F=\phi_j-\log|a_l|^2$. The function $a_l$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero on this overlap. Naturality, real-linearity, and the log-modulus clause of that node give $F^*\omega_l=D(\phi_l\circ F)=D\phi_j=\omega_j$. Thus the forms agree as tensors on every overlap and define a unique global form by using any chart at each point. Its smoothness, reality, type $(1,1)$ and closedness hold locally by the same node, hence hold globally. No holomorphic logarithm on a whole overlap has been chosen.

source.place: I §3.C (3.13)–(3.19); V §15 (15.8); VI §4 (4.4), printed pp.23–25,279,297; read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/agbook.pdf (local copy WANTED).

proof.text:
In a chart put $t=1+\sum|w_r|^2$. Differentiating gives $\partial\phi/\partial ar w_s=w_s/t$ and $H_{r ar s}=\partial^2\phi/(\partial w_r\partial ar w_s)=\delta_{rs}/t- ar w_r w_s/t^2$. Thus $H_{r ar s}=\overline{H_{s ar r}}$. For a real tangent vector $v$ with $dw_r(v)=a_r$, the definition of $D$ in [lem-sfb-local-ddbar-potential-calculus] gives $\omega(v,Jv)=\pi^{-1}\sum_{r,s}H_{r ar s}a_r ar a_s$. Expand the finite sums to obtain
$$t^2\sum_{r,s}H_{r ar s}a_r ar a_s=t\sum_r|a_r|^2-\left|\sum_r ar w_r a_right|^2=\sum_r|a_r|^2+\sum_{r<s}|w_ra_s-w_sa_r|^2.$$
For the last equality, expand each square: the diagonal terms are $\sum_{r
e s}|w_r|^2|a_s|^2$ and the cross terms subtract the off-diagonal terms in the squared absolute sum. All squares on the right are nonnegative, and $v
e0$ means some $a_r
e0$, so their first sum is positive. As $t>0$ and $\pi>0$, this proves the required positivity.

source.place: VI §4 (4.4), printed p.297; explicit coordinate Hessian and sum-of-squares verification by N8; read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/agbook.pdf (local copy WANTED).

proof.text: In the same coordinates, for $dw(v)=a$ and $dw(w')=b$, direct evaluation gives $g(v,w')=\omega(v,Jw')=\pi^{-1}\operatorname{Re}\sum_{r,s}H_{r\bar s}a_r\bar b_s$. Hermitian symmetry of $H$ makes this a symmetric real bilinear form, and replacing $a,b$ by $ia,ib$ leaves it unchanged. Positivity is step 6. It is therefore a smooth $J$-invariant positive real metric, equivalently the Hermitian metric $h(v,w')=g(v,w')-i\omega(v,w')$ on the complex tangent bundle. Its associated real form is $\omega$, already closed in step 5, which is the Kähler condition. When $n=0$, $P$ is a point, the chart is $\mathbf C^0$, all displayed differential forms and tangent vectors are zero, and the metric is the unique form on the zero vector space. The quantified positivity condition is then vacuous; no positive tangent vector or positive-dimensional assumption was used.
